title: Patel Brothers, Patidar, and Apna Bazar: Indian Grocery Goes Big-Box Across America
excerpt: Indian supermarkets are moving into former ShopRite and Buy Buy Baby locations with pharmacies, cafes, and organic produce — mirroring the H Mart playbook that transformed Asian grocery retail.
body:
Walk into the new Patidar Supermarket in Bridgewater, New Jersey, and you could be forgiven for thinking you are in a conventional American big-box grocery store. There is a pharmacy. There is a cafe. There is organic produce and an expanded array of mainstream American groceries. The only difference: the aisles are also stocked with an extraordinary range of imported Indian staples, fresh-ground masalas, and regional snacks you would struggle to find outside a bazaar in Gujarat.

## From Corner Shops to Big-Box

A decade ago, Indian grocery stores in America were modest affairs — small storefronts in strip malls, heavy on dried goods and light on frills. That era is ending. Patel Brothers, the largest Indian supermarket chain in the United States, has opened one of its largest stores in Hamilton, New Jersey, and is working on another in a former ShopRite unit in Piscataway. The new locations feature cafe seating areas and decidedly upscale decor.

Apna Bazar, a fast-growing northeastern chain with 22 locations, has announced plans to expand to Long Island and is preparing to open its largest store yet in Shrewsbury, Massachusetts — a 70,000-square-foot former Stop & Shop. And the original Patidar in North Brunswick, a cosy community anchor, now has a sibling three times its size in a former Buy Buy Baby.

## Following the H Mart Playbook

The trajectory is strikingly similar to what happened with Asian supermarkets like H Mart and 99 Ranch Market roughly fifteen years ago. Those chains expanded from niche ethnic grocers to mainstream destinations by adding ready-to-eat food, in-store eateries, and an inviting shopping experience that attracted customers well beyond the core Asian-American base.

Indian grocery retailers appear to be running the same playbook. The timing makes sense: nearly 5.5 million Americans are of Indian descent, with over 700,000 in the New York metro area alone. And the customer base is growing beyond the diaspora. Second-generation Indian-Americans and mainstream American shoppers alike are developing appetites for spices, chutneys, and ready-to-eat meals that go far beyond the "international aisle" treatment at conventional supermarkets.

## Mainstream Retailers Take Notice

The ripple effects extend beyond Indian-owned chains. Some Central Jersey ShopRites, owned by Saker ShopRites, have added freshly prepared Indian entrees to their heat-and-eat meal sections. Customers can now find dal makhani, vegetable biryani, and tandoori chicken alongside sub sandwiches and fried chicken.

Meanwhile, in the packaged goods aisle, brands like Truly Indian — an ADF Foods brand that produces approximately 150,000 hand-stretched naans daily — recently earned two NEXTY Awards finalist placements at Natural Products Expo West for its Tikka Masala Naan and Crispy Chili Mango Chutney. Indian food is not just expanding in speciality retail; it is pushing into natural, conventional, and club channels.

## The Bigger Picture for NRIs

For Indian-Americans who grew up making monthly pilgrimages to the one small Indian store in their metro area, the transformation is visceral. The new stores offer not just convenience but cultural validation — a signal that Indian food culture has arrived in the American mainstream. And for NRIs who still crave region-specific snacks, festival sweets, and Ayurvedic products, the expanding retail footprint means less compromise and more of home.
author: Diaspora Desk
